theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is the main job of a shampoo?
options: To change the natural colour of the hair a little each time
To make the hair grow faster by feeding the roots
To close the cuticle and add strength to the cortex
To lift dirt, oil and product build-up off the hair and scalp

questions.stem: How does shampoo remove oil from the hair?
options: It dries the oil out with heat as it is rinsed away
It surrounds the oil so the water can rinse it away
It turns the oil into water before it is rinsed out
It pushes the oil down into the scalp and out of sight

questions.stem: What does a pH number of 7 mean?
options: Neutral, neither acid nor alkaline
Very acid, like lemon juice
Very alkaline, like a relaxer
The product is safe for any hair

questions.stem: The skin and hair are slightly acidic. Why is an acid-balanced shampoo good for most hair?
options: It opens the cuticle wide so the hair dries faster
It strips all the natural oil out of the hair and scalp
It makes the hair swell so that it looks thicker
It is gentle and helps keep the cuticle smooth and flat

questions.stem: Which shampoo would you choose for a client with a lot of build-up from gels and oils?
options: A moisturising shampoo
A baby shampoo
A colour-care shampoo
A clarifying shampoo

questions.stem: A client has small, white, dry flakes on the scalp but no redness or sores. Which shampoo is most suitable?
options: A medicated or anti-dandruff shampoo
A clarifying shampoo used twice a day
A strong deep-cleansing dish soap
A volumising shampoo for fine hair

questions.stem: Which shampoo is best for hair that has been coloured?
options: A colour-care shampoo that is gentle on the cuticle
A deep clarifying shampoo used at every single wash
A strong anti-dandruff shampoo used every day
A high-pH shampoo that opens the cuticle wide

questions.stem: Why is a moisturising shampoo often chosen for natural, coily hair?
options: Coily hair is always oily and needs the oil stripped out
Coily hair tends to be dry and needs gentle, moist cleansing
Coily hair cannot be shampooed with any ordinary salon shampoo
Coily hair needs foam to make the curls grow much longer

questions.stem: Why should you check the client's scalp before a shampoo?
options: To find cuts, sores or infections that would stop the service
To decide how much shampoo the client will need to buy
To see whether the client washed her hair this morning
To check whether the hair has been cut at all in the last month

questions.stem: Why should you avoid scratching or massaging the scalp firmly when shampooing before a chemical service?
options: Firm massage will make the chemical work too slowly
Scratches or irritation can let the chemical burn the scalp
Firm massage will wash the colour out of the hair too fast
Massage makes the hair too soft to hold the chemical

questions.stem: How should you check the water temperature before wetting the client's hair?
options: Ask the client to put her own hand under the tap first
Turn the hot tap on full and wait for one minute
Splash a little water on the client's forehead
Test it on the inside of your wrist, then ask the client

questions.stem: What water temperature is best for most shampoos?
options: Warm, and comfortable for the client
As hot as the client can possibly stand
Ice cold, straight from the tank
Hot enough to make steam rise

questions.stem: How do you stop water running onto the client's face during a shampoo at a back-wash basin?
options: Ask the client to close her eyes and hold her breath
Cup your hand at the hairline to guide water back
Spray the water from the front towards the forehead
Use only a little water and leave the front dry

questions.stem: Which posture is best for the stylist at the basin?
options: Feet apart, back straight and the basin at a comfortable height
Bending deeply over the basin with the knees locked straight
Standing on tiptoe to reach over the top of the client's head
Leaning on the client's shoulders to steady yourself as you work

questions.stem: Which part of your hands should you use to massage the scalp during a shampoo?
options: The tips of the nails, to scrub the scalp clean
The palms only, pressing flat on the head
The knuckles, rubbing hard in straight lines
The pads of the fingers, in small circles

questions.stem: What is 'rotary' massage in a shampoo?
options: Long, smooth strokes from the forehead to the nape
Small circular movements of the finger pads on the scalp
Light tapping with the fingertips all over the head
Squeezing the lengths of the hair between the palms of both hands

questions.stem: Why do you work over the head in a set pattern when shampooing, for example from the front hairline to the back?
options: To use up the shampoo more quickly and finish sooner
To make the client fall asleep during the service
So that the whole scalp is cleaned and nothing is missed
So that the water runs onto the floor and not the gown

questions.stem: Why is a second shampoo sometimes needed?
options: The first shampoo is only there to warm up the hair and scalp
The second shampoo is needed to put colour back in
Two shampoos always make the hair grow back thicker
Very dirty hair may not be fully clean after the first one

questions.stem: How should you rinse shampoo out of the hair?
options: Quickly, for a few seconds, so that the client is not cold
Only at the ends, because the roots do not hold any shampoo
Thoroughly, until the water runs clear and no lather is left
With a towel, rubbing the lather out of the hair by hand

questions.stem: How should long, coily natural hair be shampooed to avoid tangles?
options: Pile all the hair on top of the head and rub it in circles
Shampoo it dry, then add water at the very end to rinse
Comb it through with a fine-tooth comb while it is lathered
Shampoo it in sections, working down the lengths gently

questions.stem: What is a 'co-wash'?
options: A shampoo done by two stylists working on one client at the same time
A wash done with cold water only, and no product of any kind
Washing the hair with a cleansing conditioner, not shampoo
A deep treatment left on the hair overnight

questions.stem: What does a conditioner do for the hair?
options: Cleans away oil and dirt from the scalp and hair
Changes the natural curl pattern of the hair for good
Removes old colour so new colour can be applied
Smooths the cuticle and makes the hair easier to comb

questions.stem: What is a leave-in conditioner?
options: A conditioner that stays in the hair and is not rinsed out
A conditioner that is left in the bottle to thicken overnight
A conditioner that is used only once a year at the salon
A conditioner that must be rinsed out after 30 minutes

questions.stem: Hair that feels weak and limp, and stretches too far when wet, often needs which treatment?
options: A clarifying shampoo
A protein treatment
A cold-water rinse
A strong-hold gel

questions.stem: Hair that feels hard, dry and brittle, and snaps easily, often needs which treatment?
options: A protein treatment every day
A clarifying shampoo twice
A strong-hold hairspray
A deep moisturising treatment

questions.stem: Where should a rinse-out conditioner mainly be applied?
options: Only on the scalp, rubbed in firmly
Only on the roots, then rinsed at once
Mostly on the mid-lengths and ends
On the face and neck to protect the skin

questions.stem: After applying conditioner, how should you comb it through the hair?
options: From the roots down in one firm stroke with a fine comb
Not at all, because combing wet hair always breaks it
Gently with a wide-tooth comb, starting from the ends
With a bristle brush, pulling hard through the knots

questions.stem: Why is gentle heat sometimes used during a deep conditioning treatment?
options: Gentle heat opens the cuticle a little so the treatment goes in
The heat dries the treatment onto the hair so it never needs rinsing
The heat changes the treatment into a styling gel
The heat makes the treatment work in a few seconds

questions.stem: How long should a deep conditioning treatment be left on the hair?
options: As long as possible, even overnight under the dryer
Only a few seconds, then rinse it out straight away
For the time the maker gives in the instructions
Until the client says that her scalp feels hot

questions.stem: Why is the last rinse after conditioning often done with cool or lukewarm water?
options: It makes the hair absorb more of the conditioner
It helps close the cuticle and leaves the hair shiny
It washes some of the natural colour out of the hair
It makes the hair take longer to dry after the wash

questions.stem: How should you remove water from the hair after the final rinse?
options: Rub the hair hard with a towel in circles to dry it
Wring the hair tightly like a cloth to squeeze it out
Leave it dripping and walk the client to the dryer
Squeeze and blot the hair gently with a clean towel

questions.stem: Shampoo gets into the client's eye. What should you do first?
options: Rinse the eye gently with plenty of clean, cool water
Rub the eye with a dry towel until it stops stinging
Put a drop of conditioner in the eye to soothe it
Ask the client to keep her eye shut until she goes home

questions.stem: Water has splashed on the floor around the basin. What should you do?
options: Leave it, because it will dry on its own in the heat of the day
Wipe it up at once and put out a wet floor sign if needed
Cover it with a used towel and carry on working
Tell the next client to walk around the wet area

questions.stem: Why must electrical tools be kept away from the basin area?
options: The steam from the basin makes the tools rust much more quickly
Water makes the tools heat up more slowly than usual
Water and electricity together can cause an electric shock
The tools take up space that the towels are kept in

questions.stem: Before a shampoo, why do you ask the client what products she uses at home?
options: To choose products that suit her hair and to spot any build-up
To find out which shop in town sells the cheapest hair products
To make sure she uses only the salon's products in future
To fill in the time until the water at the basin warms up

questions.stem: How much shampoo should you use?
options: Half the bottle, so that the hair is extra clean
A full palm, whatever the length of the hair
An amount to suit the hair's length and thickness
One single drop for any hair, to save money

questions.stem: What is a 'pre-poo' (pre-shampoo treatment) for natural hair?
options: Shampooing the hair twice over before the client even gets to the basin
Putting oil or conditioner on before the shampoo, to protect the hair
Drying the hair under the hood before it is shampooed
Rinsing the hair with cold water only, to wake up the scalp

questions.stem: What is one benefit of a scalp massage during the shampoo?
options: It increases the blood flow to the scalp and relaxes the client
It makes the hair grow at least 5 cm longer within one week
It removes the need for any conditioner afterwards
It changes the client's hair texture from coarse to very fine

questions.stem: When should you NOT give a firm scalp massage during a shampoo?
options: When the client has normal, healthy hair and a healthy scalp
When the client asks for a relaxing service
When the hair is long and has no tangles in it
When the scalp is tender or a chemical service is next

questions.stem: After the rinse, why should you check the hair along the back hairline and behind the ears?
options: To see if the client needs a haircut in those areas
To make sure no shampoo or conditioner is left there
To check the gown has been fastened tightly enough
To count how many grey hairs are growing there

questions.stem: After each client, what should you do with the basin?
options: Leave the hair in the drain for the cleaner at night
Run hot water into it and leave it to dry with hair in it
Remove the hair, clean the basin and wipe it with disinfectant
Cover it with a towel so that the next client cannot see the hair

questions.stem: What should be done with used towels after a shampoo?
options: Fold them and put them back on the shelf for later
Hang them on the chair to dry in the sun for the next client
Use them again for the same day if they look clean
Put them in the laundry bin to be washed before reuse

questions.stem: How should shampoos and conditioners be stored?
options: Open, in direct sunlight, so they are easy to reach
On the floor by the basin where they may be knocked over
Closed, in a cool, dry place, as the maker's label says
Mixed together in one bottle to save space on the shelf

questions.stem: Which home care advice suits a client with dry, natural hair?
options: Wash with a strong clarifying shampoo every day to keep it clean
Use a moisturising conditioner and protect the hair at night
Brush the hair dry 100 times every night before bed
Avoid all conditioners because they make hair too soft

questions.stem: Why should you write the products used on the client's record card after the service?
options: So that the client can be charged for each product used
So that the salon knows which products to throw away
So that the next stylist knows what suits her hair
So that the client cannot complain about the service

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the scale that shows how acid or alkaline a product is?
Which glands in the scalp make sebum, the hair's natural oil?
What is the name of the foam that shampoo makes when it is worked into wet hair?
What is the name of the light, smooth stroking movement used to start and finish a scalp massage?
What is the name of the kneading massage movement?
What do we call water with a lot of minerals in it, which makes it harder for shampoo to lather?
What word describes a product with a pH above 7?
What word describes hair with a raised cuticle that soaks up water very quickly?
Which piece of salon equipment gives the hair moist heat during a deep conditioning treatment?
A deep treatment must stay on for 20 minutes. It goes on at 10:50 a.m. At what time should it be rinsed off?
What is put over the hair during a deep conditioning treatment to hold in the warmth?
What is the name of the condition in which the scalp makes too much sebum, giving a very oily scalp and greasy hair?
What is the name for the back of the neck, where the hairline ends?
What word describes a disease that can be passed from one person to another?
What is the name of the cleaning ingredient in shampoo that lifts dirt and oil so that water can rinse them away?

essays.stem: Explain how shampoo cleans the hair, and why the pH of shampoos and conditioners matters.
essays.modelAnswer: Water alone cannot remove oil, because oil and water do not mix. Shampoo contains a detergent. One end of each detergent particle is attracted to water and the other end to oil and dirt. The detergent surrounds the oil and lifts it off the hair and scalp, and the water then rinses it away. Massage and lather help this happen. The pH scale runs from 0 to 14, with 7 neutral, below 7 acid and above 7 alkaline. Hair and skin are slightly acid. Alkaline products make the hair swell and lift the cuticle, which can leave it rough, tangled and dull. Acid-balanced shampoos and conditioners are gentle and help keep the cuticle smooth and flat, so the hair stays shiny and holds moisture. After an alkaline chemical service, an acid-balanced product helps bring the hair back to its normal pH.
markingPoints: Explains that oil and water do not mix, so a detergent is needed
Detergent surrounds the oil and dirt so water can rinse them away
Explains the pH scale: 7 neutral, below acid, above alkaline
Alkaline products swell the hair and lift the cuticle
Acid-balanced products are gentle and keep the cuticle smooth

essays.stem: Describe how you would choose a shampoo and conditioner for three clients: one with oily hair and heavy product build-up, one with dry, coily natural hair, and one with coloured hair.
essays.modelAnswer: For every client I first do a consultation and check the scalp and hair. For the client with oily hair and heavy build-up, I would use a clarifying shampoo to remove the build-up, perhaps with two shampoos, and then a light rinse-out conditioner on the ends only, so the hair does not feel heavy. I would advise her not to use a clarifying shampoo too often at home. For the client with dry, coily natural hair, I would choose a gentle moisturising shampoo, or a co-wash, worked through in sections, and a rich moisturising conditioner or deep treatment, followed by a leave-in conditioner. For the client with coloured hair, I would use a colour-care shampoo that is acid-balanced and gentle, and a colour-care conditioner, so the colour does not fade quickly. In each case I would follow the maker's instructions and record the products used.
markingPoints: Consultation and hair and scalp check before choosing
Oily hair with build-up: clarifying shampoo and light conditioner on the ends
Dry, coily hair: moisturising shampoo or co-wash and a rich or leave-in conditioner
Coloured hair: gentle, acid-balanced colour-care products
Follows the maker's instructions and records the products

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how to shampoo a client at a back-wash basin, from seating her to wrapping her hair in a towel.
essays.modelAnswer: After the consultation and gowning, I seat the client at the basin and lower her head back gently, with a folded towel at the neck for comfort, and check that she is comfortable. I run the water and test it on the inside of my wrist, then ask the client if it suits her. I wet the hair fully, cupping my hand at the hairline to keep water off her face. I put a suitable amount of shampoo in my palm, spread it over my hands and apply it evenly. Using the pads of my fingers, I massage the scalp in small circles, working in a set pattern from the front hairline to the nape, and lift the head gently to reach the back. I rinse until the water runs clear, and repeat if needed. After conditioning, I squeeze out the water, wrap the hair in a clean towel and help the client sit up slowly.
markingPoints: Seats the client comfortably with neck support and checks comfort
Tests the water on the wrist and asks the client
Wets the hair fully and keeps water off the face
Applies shampoo evenly and massages with finger pads in a set pattern
Rinses until clear, then squeezes out water, wraps in a towel and sits the client up slowly

essays.stem: Describe the massage movements used during a shampoo and conditioning service. Say when each is used, and when massage should be kept light or left out.
essays.modelAnswer: Effleurage is a light, smooth stroking movement with the palms or fingers. It is used to spread the shampoo or conditioner and to start and finish the massage, and it is relaxing. Rotary movements are small, firm circles with the pads of the fingers. They are used during the shampoo to loosen dirt and oil and to stimulate the scalp. Friction is a quicker, deeper rubbing with the finger pads, used on an oily scalp during the shampoo, but never with the nails. Petrissage is a gentle kneading of the scalp, used during a conditioning treatment to help it work in and relax the client. Massage should be kept light, or left out, if the client is having a chemical service next, if the scalp is sensitive, sore or has cuts, if the hair is very fragile, or if the client asks for less pressure. Firm massage on an oily scalp can make it more oily.
markingPoints: Effleurage: light stroking to spread product and start and finish
Rotary: small circles with finger pads during the shampoo
Friction or petrissage described correctly, with when each is used
Never uses the nails
Keeps massage light or leaves it out before a chemical service, on a sensitive or broken scalp, or for fragile or oily hair

essays.stem: Describe how to apply a deep conditioning treatment with heat, from choosing the product to the final rinse.
essays.modelAnswer: During the consultation I check the hair's porosity and elasticity, and ask about chemical services and home care. If the hair is weak and stretches too much, I choose a protein treatment; if it is dry and brittle, a moisturising one. I shampoo the hair and blot out the extra water, because a treatment works best on clean, damp hair. I divide the hair into sections and apply the treatment from the mid-lengths to the ends, then to the roots if the maker says, and comb it through gently with a wide-tooth comb. I cover the hair with a plastic cap and put the client under a hood dryer or steamer on the setting the maker gives, checking she is comfortable. I time the treatment as the maker says. Then I let the hair cool for a moment and rinse thoroughly with lukewarm water, finishing with a cooler rinse to smooth the cuticle.
markingPoints: Uses porosity and elasticity tests to choose protein or moisture
Applies to clean, damp hair in sections and combs through gently
Covers with a cap and uses gentle heat, checking the client's comfort
Times the treatment as the maker says
Rinses thoroughly, ending with a cooler rinse

essays.stem: Explain the difference between rinse-out, leave-in, protein and moisturising conditioners, and say when you would use each.
essays.modelAnswer: A rinse-out conditioner is put on after the shampoo, left for a minute or two and rinsed off. It smooths the cuticle, cuts tangles and static, and suits most hair as part of every wash. A leave-in conditioner is put on after the final rinse and not rinsed out. It gives lasting softness and protection, and suits dry, curly, coily or chemically treated hair, often before styling. A protein treatment puts protein back into hair that is weak, limp or stretches too much, for example after colour or a relaxer. It is used now and then, not at every wash, because too much protein can leave hair hard. A moisturising treatment adds water and softness to hair that is dry, hard or brittle, which is common in natural, coily hair and in our hot climate. Many clients need a balance of protein and moisture, so I check the hair each visit.
markingPoints: Rinse-out: after shampoo, rinsed off; smooths and detangles; for most hair
Leave-in: not rinsed out; for dry, curly, coily or treated hair
Protein: for weak, limp or over-stretchy hair; used now and then
Moisturising: for dry, hard or brittle hair
Mentions a balance of protein and moisture, checked each visit

essays.stem: Describe how to shampoo and condition long, tightly coiled natural hair without causing tangles and breakage.
essays.modelAnswer: First I do a consultation and check the scalp. Before wetting the hair, I gently finger-detangle it and divide it into four to eight sections, twisting or clipping each one so that it stays apart. I may put on a little oil or conditioner as a pre-shampoo treatment to protect the lengths. I wet the hair well, then apply a moisturising shampoo to the scalp, one section at a time. I massage the scalp with my finger pads and let the lather run down the lengths, squeezing gently rather than rubbing or piling the hair up. I rinse each section well. I then apply conditioner to each section and detangle it with my fingers or a wide-tooth comb, working from the ends up to the roots. I rinse with lukewarm, then cooler water, blot with a towel or a soft cotton T-shirt, and apply a leave-in conditioner before styling.
markingPoints: Detangles gently and divides the hair into sections before wetting
Uses a pre-shampoo treatment or protects the lengths
Shampoos the scalp in sections, squeezing the lengths and not piling or rubbing
Conditions and detangles each section from ends to roots with fingers or a wide-tooth comb
Rinses well, blots gently and applies a leave-in conditioner

essays.stem: Explain the safety points a stylist must follow during a shampoo service, for the client and for herself.
essays.modelAnswer: For the client, I check the scalp for cuts or infection before starting. I test the water on my wrist and ask the client, so she is not scalded or chilled, and I keep a hand on the tap in case the temperature changes. I support her neck with a towel and help her sit up slowly, as some people feel dizzy. I keep water and shampoo away from her eyes and rinse at once with clean water if any gets in. For myself, I stand with feet apart, a straight back and the basin at a good height, so that I do not strain my back. I wear gloves if a product could irritate my skin, and dry my hands well afterwards to prevent dermatitis. For everyone, I wipe up spills at once so no one slips, and I keep electrical tools and cables away from the water. I follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Checks the scalp first and tests the water temperature on the wrist and with the client
Supports the neck, sits the client up slowly, protects the eyes
Good posture at the basin to protect the stylist's back
Gloves where needed and dries hands to prevent dermatitis
Wipes up spills and keeps electrical tools away from water

essays.stem: Describe how you would clean and leave the basin area after a shampoo service, and how shampoos and conditioners should be stored.
essays.modelAnswer: When the client has left the basin, I remove hair from the basin and drain trap, wearing gloves, and put it in the bin. I clean the basin, taps and spray hose with detergent and water, then wipe them with a disinfectant, following the maker's instructions for the contact time. I wipe the basin chair and neck rest. Used towels and gowns go in the laundry bin. Combs and brushes are washed, rinsed and put in disinfectant. I dry the floor around the basin and put out a wet floor sign if it is still damp. I put the lids back on all products, wipe any drips off the bottles, and put them back in their place. Shampoos and conditioners are stored closed and upright, in a cool, dry place, out of direct sunlight, as the label says. I use the oldest stock first and report anything that is running low.
markingPoints: Removes hair from the basin and drain with gloves on
Cleans then disinfects the basin, taps, hose and chair
Used towels to laundry, tools washed and disinfected
Dries the floor and uses a wet floor sign if needed
Stores products closed, upright, cool, dry and out of the sun; uses oldest stock first

essays.stem: Explain the home care advice you would give after a shampoo and conditioning service to (a) a client with dry, damaged hair and (b) a client with an oily scalp. Say why.
essays.modelAnswer: For the client with dry, damaged hair, I would suggest a gentle moisturising shampoo, not washing too often, and using a conditioner every wash with a deep treatment about every one or two weeks, as the maker suggests. A leave-in conditioner helps keep the hair soft. She should cut down on heat and use a heat protectant, detangle gently with a wide-tooth comb, and protect her hair at night with a satin bonnet or pillowcase. This puts back moisture and stops more breakage. For the client with an oily scalp, I would suggest a gentle shampoo for oily hair, washing as often as she needs, with warm, not hot, water. She should put conditioner only on the ends, avoid heavy oils and greases on the scalp, and avoid hard scrubbing, which can make the scalp produce more oil. For both clients, I would suggest suitable products and book a return visit.
markingPoints: Dry hair: moisturising shampoo and regular conditioning or deep treatment
Dry hair: less heat, gentle detangling and night protection, with the reason
Oily scalp: shampoo for oily hair and warm, not hot, water
Oily scalp: conditioner on ends only, no heavy oils, no hard scrubbing, with the reason
Suggests suitable products and a return visit

practical1.title: Shampoo and conditioning service on two different hair types
practical1.brief: Work as a group of 4 or 5 in the Centre's salon. Each member gives a full shampoo and rinse-out conditioning service to a group partner or a model who agrees. Between you, the clients must include at least one with natural, curly or coily hair and one with straight, wavy or relaxed hair. Each stylist does a consultation and scalp check, chooses and explains the products, gowns the client, tests the water, shampoos with the right massage, conditions and detangles, then towel-blots and wraps the hair, and fills in a record card. While one member works, another takes the photos and a third checks the steps on the group's checklist; change roles so that everyone does each job. Photograph only the hair, hands and basin area, never faces, unless the model agrees and the Centre allows it. Hand in once for the whole group when every service is finished and the basins are clean.
materials: Shampoos and conditioners for different hair types (moisturising, clarifying, colour-care)
Clean gowns, towels and waterproof capes
Neck rest or rolled towel for the basin
Gloves, disinfectant for the basin and surfaces, and a laundry bin

The client gowned and seated comfortably at the basin
Testing the water on the inside of the wrist
Shampoo massage with the finger pads
Conditioner being detangled through with a wide-tooth comb, from the ends
The hair blotted and wrapped in a clean towel
The basin cleaned and the area left dry
checklist: Carried out a consultation and scalp check and chose suitable products
Gowned the client correctly and made sure she was comfortable at the basin
Tested the water on the wrist and checked with the client
Kept water off the client's face, ears and clothes
Massaged with the finger pads in a set pattern, never the nails
Rinsed thoroughly, conditioned and detangled gently from the ends
Blotted and wrapped the hair and helped the client sit up slowly
Filled in the record card and cleaned the basin and tools
safety: Test the water temperature before it touches the client, and keep a hand near the tap
Wipe up water on the floor at once and use a wet floor sign
Keep all electrical tools and cables away from the basin
Stop and tell the assessor if a client has cuts, sores or signs of infection on the scalp
Rinse at once with clean, cool water if shampoo gets into an eye

practical2.title: Sectioned shampoo and deep conditioning treatment on natural hair
practical2.brief: Work as a group of 4 or 5 in the Centre's salon. Each member gives a sectioned shampoo and a deep conditioning treatment with heat to a group partner or a model with natural, curly or coily hair who agrees. Each stylist does a porosity and elasticity test, chooses a protein or moisturising treatment and explains why, detangles and sections the hair before the shampoo, shampoos and rinses section by section, applies the treatment, covers the hair with a plastic cap and times it under a hood dryer or steamer as the maker says. Then the stylist rinses, applies a leave-in conditioner and puts the hair into large twists or plaits to keep it stretched. Members share the dryers and steamers and plan the order together. Each member photographs another member's work. Photograph only the hair, hands and work area, never faces, unless the model agrees and the Centre allows it. Hand in once for the whole group when every service is finished and the area is clean.
materials: Moisturising shampoo and a light oil or conditioner for pre-shampoo
Protein and moisturising deep treatments, with the maker's instructions
Wide-tooth combs, sectioning clips and snag-free bands
Gloves, disinfectant and a laundry bin

checklist: Carried out porosity and elasticity tests and chose a suitable treatment
Detangled gently and sectioned the hair before wetting
Shampooed section by section without piling or rubbing the hair
Applied the treatment evenly and covered the hair
Used heat and timing as the maker says and checked the client's comfort
Rinsed thoroughly, finishing with a cooler rinse
Applied a leave-in conditioner and left the hair stretched in neat twists or plaits
Cleaned the basin, tools and dryer or steamer after use
safety: Follow the maker's instructions for each treatment, the dryer and the steamer
Check the dryer or steamer is working and set it before the client sits under it
Check on each client under heat every few minutes and ask if she is comfortable
Keep cables tidy and away from water, and wipe up spills at once
